text: Site-to-site VPN, from the last lesson, is an encrypted tunnel that still crosses the public internet. ExpressRoute and Direct Connect solve a different problem entirely: a private, dedicated physical connection between your on-prem network and the cloud provider's network that never touches the public internet at all, for the entire trip.

There's no IPsec encryption configured on these connections, and that's not a gap -- it's because there's no shared public medium in the middle to encrypt against in the first place. The traffic simply never enters the public internet. This isn't a faster version of a VPN; it's a different physical path, with a different cost model and a much longer provisioning timeline, which Lesson 23 covers in detail.

You don't click a button to get one. You work with a connectivity provider -- a telecom or colocation partner operating at an ExpressRoute location or Direct Connect location -- who provisions the physical cross-connect between your network and a dedicated port, typically 1, 10, or 100 Gbps, on the cloud provider's edge router. That physical link is what Azure calls an ExpressRoute circuit and AWS calls a Direct Connect connection, and it's billed separately from the data that flows across it.

Azure splits what that circuit can reach into peering types: Private Peering reaches your VNets, Microsoft Peering reaches Microsoft 365 and other Microsoft services running outside your own VNets. AWS uses a Direct Connect Gateway when one physical connection needs to reach VPCs across multiple regions rather than just the one it was provisioned in.

Because the traffic rides a dedicated path instead of sharing the internet with everyone else, both services deliver more consistent latency and bandwidth -- no competing with unrelated congestion. Some compliance frameworks specifically require that data never cross the public internet at all, encrypted or not, which only a dedicated circuit satisfies. Next: when a VPN is actually enough, and when it isn't.
